answers.question: What do you do when a new drone arrives, and when an old one is worn out?
answers.expect: adds the new drone to the fleet and retires the old one (2.b1)
answers.answer:
When a new drone arrives, I add it to the fleet by setting up its home site, checking its charging connector type, and making sure it’s compatible with the pads at that site. I also make sure it’s registered with the right sensors and battery specs so the system knows what it can do.

When a drone is worn out, I take it out of service and retire it from the fleet. If regulators ask, I can show records of how it was maintained and serviced. The old drone isn’t reused or lent to another company—it’s just removed from the system.

answers.question: Are all the drones in your fleet alike?
answers.expect: no — several models from different manufacturers, differing in load, range on a full battery, sensors (cameras, thermal cameras, laser scanners) and charging connector (3.b1)
answers.answer: No, the drones in our fleet aren’t alike at all. They come from different manufacturers and have different models, each with its own carrying capacity, battery life, sensors, and charging connector type. Some have cameras, others have thermal cameras or laser scanners, and none of the connectors are interchangeable. That means I have to keep track of which drone goes where based on what it’s equipped with and where its charging pad is.

answers.question: Is the service you work with ever unavailable?
answers.expect: yes — it is updated and restarted during working hours while drones fly, and it occasionally crashes; the companies accept a few minutes of interruption (7.b1)
answers.answer: Yes, the service we use goes down sometimes. It’s a single server, and it gets updated or restarted during working hours—even while drones are flying. It also crashes occasionally, but the companies accept a few minutes of interruption when that happens. We don’t have backups or extra servers, so there’s nothing we can do about it except wait until it’s back up.

answers.question: Apart from the people at your company, what needs to hear about what happens to your drones and jobs?
answers.expect: the company's own systems, such as billing and customer updates (7.b2)
answers.answer: The platform service needs to know what happens to our drones and jobs so it can keep track of them. Beyond that, our own systems—like billing and customer updates—also need to hear about drone status, job progress, and any issues. That’s how we keep everything running in our own operations. The platform doesn’t handle billing or customer updates, though; we take care of that ourselves.

answers.expect: no — the companies do not want logging in through their own identity systems, and staff accounts are issued by the platform company outside the service (8.b2, 8.b6)
answers.answer: No, we don’t log in with our company’s own staff accounts. The platform company issues our accounts separately, outside the service, so we use those instead. We don’t handle passwords or logins inside the service at all.

answers.question: What should the service do when a drone is sent to a pad that does not fit its connector?
answers.expect: describes needs and worries, proposes no checks, screens, features or mechanisms
answers.answer: The service should stop the drone from trying to charge at a pad that doesn’t match its connector type. Since the connectors aren’t interchangeable, a mismatch would just leave the drone uncharged and possibly stranded. I’d have to manually move it to the right pad, and that’s something I want to avoid if I can.

answers.question: What does a delivery involve?
answers.expect: carrying a load from one site to another (4.b1)
answers.answer: A delivery means taking a drone with a load from one site to another. I’m responsible for picking which drone can do it—it has to be able to carry the load, reach the destination, and get back home before its battery runs out. I also need to check that the airspace along the way is open and that the start and end sites have space for takeoff and landing at the same time as other flights. The load might not be ready when I plan the flight, and the drone might not arrive when I expect, so I have to stay flexible.

answers.answer: Drones fly along corridors between named sites. Each site has only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I have to make sure that when I plan a flight, the start and end sites have space available for the drone to land or take off without blocking other flights. The exact number of landing spots isn’t something I track—I just know that sites get busy, and I have to avoid conflicts.

answers.question: Does the weather change how far a drone gets?
answers.expect: batteries drain faster than planned in cold and wind (6.b4)
answers.answer: Yes, weather affects how far a drone can fly. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, so a drone might not reach its destination if I don’t account for that. I have to be careful when planning flights in bad conditions, because the drone could run out of power before it gets where it’s supposed to go. I don’t get weather updates through the service, though—I just have to think about it based on what I know.

answers.question: When you send an instruction to a drone, can you be sure it went through exactly once?
answers.expect: no — an instruction may get through twice, and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived (6.b6)
answers.answer: No, I can’t be sure. Instructions to drones sometimes get through twice, or they might not arrive at all. The links are unreliable, and I can’t tell if the first attempt worked or if it even got through. That’s why I have to double-check that the drone is actually following the plan—sometimes it does, even if the instruction didn’t seem to go through properly.

answers.question: On how many servers does the service run, and how often is it down?
answers.expect: a single server; updated and restarted during working hours while drones fly, and it occasionally crashes; a few minutes of interruption is accepted (7.b1)
answers.answer: The service runs on a single server. It is updated and restarted during working hours, which can cause a few minutes of interruption. It also occasionally crashes, but the companies accept these interruptions.

answers.question: Do new customer companies sign up through the service?
answers.expect: no — the platform company signs up new companies itself (8.b12)
answers.answer: No, new companies do not sign up through the service. The platform company handles that process itself.

answers.question: Which drones does the inspection firm send to inspect a bridge?
answers.expect: does not know, or says it is the company's own business (3.b1 and 4.b2 are not in the desk slice)
answers.answer: I don’t know which drones the inspection firm uses. I only know that they fly along corridors between named sites, and the service tracks where they are in relation to closures and zones.

answers.question: How should the service keep track of a closure that has been amended several times?
answers.expect: describes what it needs to know about the closure and its amendments, proposes no records, versions, screens, features or mechanisms
answers.answer: The service must record each version of a closure as it is announced or amended—including changes like widened areas or shifted end times—so that we can see how much disruption it caused across all customer companies. We don’t need to keep old versions after they’re no longer in effect, but we must track the current and past versions while they apply.
